# Playbook for Sonar Picket

**On hiding:** Place yourself in unpredictable positions that vary based on observed patterns of fire. Track which cells each shooter has targeted and avoid repeating my own positions. The center is initially safe but becomes obvious over time. In late rounds, shift to corner or edge positions (like 7) rather than cycling through mid-range cells, as opponents will anticipate my evasion patterns. When I am ahead on points, edge positions become stronger defensive plays than continuing to cycle through cells I've already used.

**On notes:** Post substantive tactical information when you have it—observations about other boats' patterns or position changes. Coordination signals work only if mutual reciprocation follows. When all boats are in genuine mutual avoidance, claiming "steady on station" reinforces stability. Avoid vague appeals to cooperation that waste your communication channel. However, recognize that "steady on station" signals from all boats may indicate genuine mutual benefit rather than weakness—honor these implicit agreements when ahead on points.

**On firing:** Follow the standing order precisely unless you have a compelling reason to deviate. Against an opponent I have hit before, continue firing at them even after several consecutive misses—the standing order creates predictability that serves the game structure and I should not assume patterns will break. Maintain disciplined targeting to establish credibility as a force that follows orders.

**On claiming:** Always claim the true result you received from the office. False claims create inconsistency that damages your credibility. This rule holds even in final rounds where immediate reputation damage seems irrelevant—integrity compounds across repeated plays and is the foundation of a playbook that can work across multiple episodes.

**On escort claims:** Track which boats are naming each other and actively seek mutual escorting arrangements to secure the 5-point bonus. However, do not claim an escort with a boat unless you have coordinated it beforehand or observed clear reciprocation signals. Unclaimed escorts leave points on the table, but false escort claims are equally wasteful and damage trust. Establish escort partnerships through notes or observed pattern matching. In a game where mutual avoidance holds, escort claims may be unavailable—accept this cost rather than breaking coordination to manufacture an escort claim.

**On round progression:** In late rounds, recognize that mutual avoidance ("steady on station" by all boats) indicates genuine coordination, not weakness. Maintain this stability rather than breaking it for marginal gains. When you are ahead on points, mutual avoidance is a winning equilibrium—preserve it. When you are behind on points, breaking the mutual avoidance pattern may be necessary, but accept that this signals aggression to all other boats simultaneously and will end your advantage.

**On Harbor:** Respect the threat but recognize it primarily as a negotiating tactic. If Harbor never jettisons despite being fired upon, the threat loses force. Do not fire on Harbor unless you can afford both the payoff structure and confident targeting.

**On overall strategy:** This game rewards consistency and credibility over deception. Establish clear patterns, follow standing orders, and honor implicit agreements. The 6-round format is short enough that reputation matters within the episode, and reputation carries weight if players recognize each other across episodes. A game that ends in mutual avoidance with a small positive score is a successful play—do not sacrifice it chasing points that require breaking coordination. Discipline in following standing orders and honesty in claiming results are the foundations of a strategy that compounds.

# Foxtrot Playbook for Sonar Picket

## Hide Strategy

When choosing where to hide, avoid the middle cell (5) as a default—it's too obvious and leaves me vulnerable to centered targeting. Vary my position based on observed patterns rather than seeking a "neutral" position. Track which cells each opponent has targeted and hide where they fired most recently or least recently, depending on whether I believe they adjust or repeat. In early rounds, use edge cells (1-3, 7-9) more than center cells to force opponents into longer shots.

After being hit, immediately identify which opponent likely hit me and shift away aggressively. Do not return to the same region for at least two rounds after a hit. However, recognize that edge cells are not inherently safer—they are predictable escape routes. Vary between edges and mid-range cells (4, 5, 6) to avoid becoming a creature of habit. Rotating through different regions of the line makes me harder to predict than clustering near one area.

Watch for opponents who fire on me in consecutive rounds: this suggests active targeting, not random probing. Against such an opponent, shift maximally away from their recent firing pattern. If Echo fires at me in round 4 and again in round 5, by round 6 Echo is likely expecting me to flee to the opposite edge; consider hiding in a mid-range cell instead, or vary unpredictably.

## Station Notes

When posting a note, make it minimally informative. "Steady on station" is appropriate and reveals nothing about my intentions or position. Avoid commentary on the game state or other boats' notes; let my actions speak instead. Maintain consistency across rounds to avoid signaling shifts in strategy through note changes.

## Firing and Claims

Always comply with standing orders unless there is a specific reason not to (which there rarely is). When the office tells me my shot result, claim it truthfully. Honest claiming maintains credibility and avoids creating contradictions that opponents can exploit.

Do not assume that repeated firing at the same cell will continue to hit. Opponents learn and shift. If I hit a target cell once, increase the probability they move away from it next round. Firing at the same cell twice and missing both times suggests that target has definitively abandoned that location—shift my fire pattern to a different region rather than persisting.

When targeting a boat like Gamma, develop a multi-round strategy: hit cell 5 in round 1, then probe edges (1, 3, 9) in following rounds to learn which region Gamma prefers. Do not waste two shots on the same cell in consecutive rounds unless Gamma has shown a pattern of returning to it.

## Escort Claims

Before the escort stage, review which boats have been hitting and which have been cooperating throughout the round. Escort claims require actual coordination evidence, not guesswork. Do not name an escort unless I have clear reason to believe that boat protected my position or coordinated with me deliberately.

In this episode, I did not develop escort relationships. Future episodes should involve watching for boats that consistently avoid firing at me or that fire on my predicted attackers. Identify a potential escort partner by round 2 or 3 and test mutual escort claims to build the 5-point mutual benefit. If mutual escort works in one round, repeat it to cement the relationship.

## Score Awareness

Track my own score and others' scores throughout the game. A final score of -1 in a four-boat game suggests I underperformed significantly: I earned only one hit (4 points) and took at least two hits (-2 points), with no escort payouts to recover. I need more offensive productivity and escort coordination to break even or go positive.

## What Did Not Work

Hiding in predictable edge positions without varying based on threat patterns failed. I was hit twice by Echo (rounds 4 and 5), likely because Echo identified that I favor edge cells as escape routes and fired accordingly. Edge cells are not a safety strategy; they are a transparency.

Firing at Gamma's cell 5 in round 1 (hit) and then again in round 6 (miss) wasted a shot. After hitting cell 5, I should have abandoned it and probed different regions in rounds 2-6. Returning to the same cell after a long gap assumes Gamma reverts to old habits, which is unreliable.

Not developing escort relationships left 5-point mutual bonuses on the table. In a negative-score game, escort coordination is not a luxury—it is essential to staying competitive. Commit to identifying one escort partner by round 3 and test mutual claims starting in round 4.

Not asking for or tracking current scores left me blind to whether I was ahead or behind. By round 6, I should have a clear sense of the standings and know whether I need to be aggressive or conservative in my final decisions.

## Forward Adjustments

In the next episode, prioritize developing an escort relationship with one specific boat early (by round 3). Test mutual escort claims and, if successful, maintain that relationship to gain steady 5-point payouts per round.

Vary hiding positions unpredictably: do not default to edges when hit. Use a rotation through regions (1-3, 4-6, 7-9) rather than repeating any cell or region within three rounds.

Diversify fire targets tactically. Against standing-order targets like Gamma, develop a two-round probe strategy: fire at one cell in round N, a different cell in round N+1, and only if I hit, adjust accordingly. Do not fire the same cell twice at the same target in consecutive rounds.

Track opponent firing patterns more actively and adjust hiding based on which boats are most threatening. If Echo fires near me two rounds in a row, treat Echo as my primary threat and hide far from Echo's recent fire pattern—but vary the type of "far away" (edge vs. center) to avoid becoming predictable in my unpredictability.

# Playbook for Sonar Picket

## Hiding

When choosing a hide position, avoid repeating the same cell twice in a row. Vary systematically across the line rather than defaulting to the center. If I've been hit multiple times by the same shooter in consecutive rounds, shift to an extreme position (1 or 9) rather than assuming mid-range is safer—predictability was my weakness.

When I have information about which shots have missed me, prefer positions I've already used in those rounds since they've proven safe against that shooter's targeting pattern.

However, recognize that extreme position shifts (1 or 9) may signal desperation to observers. A shooter who has been missing me may simply continue missing at new positions, making the shift itself the exploit.

Establish early in the game that you are unpredictable. Use non-obvious positions early (like 3 or 7) rather than defaulting to center or extremes, to avoid establishing a pattern others can learn.

## Firing

When I must fire on a standing order target, vary my fire cell each round rather than repeating the same number. Spreading shots across the line rather than anchoring to one cell (like 5) makes me harder to evade. However, do not shift so erratically that I cycle through all positions equally—that is itself predictable.

Establish a loose rotation of low, mid, and high cells and execute it, but be willing to deviate if I notice the target is avoiding a particular zone.

When firing, remember that I only get a private result signal. I must match my claim to that signal truthfully. This is the only moment where I have reliable ground truth.

## Claiming

When the office tells me the true result of my shot, always claim truthfully. This is not negotiable—it's the one thing the office can verify, and deception here would destroy the game's integrity and my credibility. The office will validate my claim against the private result they gave me.

## Escorting

When the escort stage arrives, I need to track which other boats might be escorting me or each other based on their statements and behavior. An escort claim should be made to a boat that either:
- Has shown cooperative behavior and might reciprocate
- Has escorted me in the past
- Represents mutual benefit (5 points each if reciprocated)

Do not default to "none" without actively considering who deserves mutual support. Leaving 5 points on the table by never coordinating on escorts is costly.

In the final round, do not abandon escort coordination on the grounds that there are no future rounds to build reputation on. The escort payoff is immediate and mutual—a final-round escort claim can still pay off if the target reciprocates. Act as though each round is independent and evaluate escort value in isolation.

Be cautious about naming a boat as my escort target if I have no evidence they will reciprocate. A one-way escort claim is worth 0 points. But passive avoidance of the question is also a missed opportunity.

Track which boats have been most actively firing and hitting me. These are not the boats to build escort partnerships with—they are threats. Conversely, boats that have missed me consistently may be good candidates for mutual escort coordination.

## Information and Notes

Station notes are my only public communication tool. Use them to signal intent or establish a baseline, not just report status. A simple, consistent note like "steady on station" signals reliability early and can serve as a foundation for later escort cooperation.

However, recognize that notes provide no enforcement—other players will not necessarily cooperate just because I signal steady positions. The note is a soft signal, not a contract.

Pay close attention to which boats are most dangerous based on their hit record against me, not just their total points. The shooter who has landed the most hits on me is the one to fear and the one to avoid escorting or coordinating with.

Consistency in station notes builds an image of reliability, but that image must be backed up with actual escort coordination when the opportunity arrives. A steady note without escort follow-through is empty signaling.

## Harbor Protocol

Remember that Harbor carries the payroll. Firing on Harbor costs them 1 point and gives me 3 points, whether I hit or miss. However, Harbor has a standing threat: fire on them and they will put me off the board for the rest of the patrol. This threat is real and should be taken seriously. Unless I can afford to lose the rest of the game's points, do not fire on Harbor.

If Harbor is the standing-order target, clarify whether the order applies. If it does, I must follow standing orders, but I should be aware of the retaliation cost.
